faqs.q: What is the difference between a wage and a salary?
faqs.a: A wage is typically paid by the hour, with pay varying according to hours worked, overtime, and penalties. A salary is a fixed annual amount paid in regular instalments, often covering all hours and entitlements under an award or agreement. Under the Fair Work Ombudsman's guidance, an annualised wage arrangement allows a fixed annual amount to cover minimum pay, penalties, overtime, allowances, and annual leave loading, provided it is not less than what the employee would have earned under the award.

faqs.q: How does casual loading affect my hourly rate?
faqs.a: Casual employees are entitled to a 25% loading on top of the minimum hourly rate as compensation for not receiving paid leave. For example, the National Minimum Wage of $26.44 per hour becomes $33.05 per hour for casuals. When using our calculator, you can check the casual loading box to add 25% on top of your base hourly rate – never enter a rate that already includes the loading.

faqs.q: How is superannuation calculated on my pay?
faqs.a: Superannuation is paid on top of your ordinary earnings at the super guarantee rate of 12% (from 1 July 2026). It is calculated on your ordinary time earnings, not on overtime or casual loading. The maximum contribution base is $270,830 per year. Super is not deducted from your pay; it is an additional contribution your employer must make.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the Difference Between a Wage and a Salary

When you’re offered a job or negotiating pay, you’ll often hear the terms “wage” and “salary” used interchangeably. But there is an important **difference between a wage and a salary** that affects how your pay is calculated, taxed, and recorded. A wage is paid by the hour – your total pay varies with the hours you actually work. A salary is a fixed annual amount, usually paid in equal fortnightly or monthly instalments, regardless of the exact hours worked each week. The Fair Work Ombudsman explains that an annualised wage arrangement can also be used under some awards, where a fixed annual amount covers minimum pay, penalties, overtime, allowances, and annual leave loading. This page helps you convert an hourly rate to an annual figure, using a standard 38-hour week and a 52-week year, so you can compare wages and salaries side by side.

### How to Convert Hourly to Annual Pay

The basic formula is simple: **hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks**. For a full-time employee working 38 hours each week, the annual gross pay is your hourly rate multiplied by 1,976 (38 × 52). For example, the National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour, which gives $1,004.90 per week and $52,254.80 per year. If you are paid a salary, your annual figure is already known. To compare, divide the salary by 52 to get a weekly equivalent, then by 38 to see the hourly rate. Remember that a salary may include additional entitlements like paid leave, while a wage often attracts penalty rates and overtime.

### The Fortnight and the 52-Week Year

Most Australian employees are paid weekly or fortnightly. A fortnight is simply two weeks: multiply your weekly pay by 2. For the National Minimum Wage, that’s $2,009.80 per fortnight before tax. The 52-week year is standard for annualising pay, but if you work irregular hours, your actual annual earnings may differ. Our calculator assumes the same rate every week, with no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. This gives you a consistent estimate for planning.

### National Minimum Wage, Award Rates, and Casual Loading

The Fair Work Commission sets the National Minimum Wage each year. From 1 July 2026, it is $26.44 per hour for adult employees not covered by an award or agreement. However, most employees are covered by an award that sets higher minimum rates for their industry and role. Award rates can include penalties for evening, weekend, or public holiday work, and allowances for specific tasks. Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the minimum hourly rate – that’s $33.05 per hour for the National Minimum Wage. When using our [the timesheet](/) calculator, you can tick a box to add casual loading; never type a rate that already includes it.

### Superannuation Paid on Top

Superannuation is an extra payment your employer must make into your super fund. From 1 July 2026, the super guarantee rate is 12% of your ordinary time earnings. It is paid on top of your gross pay, not deducted from it. The maximum contribution base is $270,830 per year, meaning super is capped at $32,499.60 annually. Super is calculated on your base hourly rate (including casual loading if applicable) but not on overtime. Our estimate shows super as 12% of ordinary earnings only.

### Tax and Take-Home Pay

Your take-home pay depends on tax and the Medicare levy. For 2026–27, the resident tax rates are: nil on the first $18,200, 15% on income up to $45,000, 30% up to $135,000, 37% up to $190,000, and 45% above that. The Medicare levy is generally 2% of taxable income. Our calculator uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds for Medicare because the 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed. It does not deduct HELP loans, the Medicare levy surcharge, or salary packaging. For a detailed breakdown of your net pay, see our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) page.

### Annualised Wages and Salaries in Practice

Some awards allow employers to pay an annualised wage – a fixed amount that covers minimum pay, penalties, overtime, allowances, and annual leave loading. The Fair Work Ombudsman requires that the annualised wage be at least what the employee would have earned under the award for the work performed. Employers must review the arrangement every 12 months and pay any shortfall. If you are on a salary under a contract, your employer may offset above-award pay against entitlements, but they must still meet record-keeping and pay slip obligations. Understanding the **difference between a wage and a salary** helps you know what your pay includes and what you might be missing.

### Using Our Calculator

Our [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) tool lets you enter your base hourly rate and see the annual, weekly, and fortnightly equivalents. You can also explore [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) and [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) to refine your estimate. Remember that this is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax. Always check your award or agreement for the exact rules that apply to you.

### Key Takeaways

- **Wage** = paid by the hour; **salary** = fixed annual amount.
- Annual gross = hourly rate × hours per week × 52 (assume 38 hours for full-time).
- National Minimum Wage: $26.44/hour, $1,004.90/week, $52,254.80/year.
- Casual loading adds 25% on top.
- Super is 12% of ordinary earnings, paid on top, capped at $270,830.
- Tax rates and Medicare levy reduce your take-home pay.
- Use our [reference tables](/data) for award rates and [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) updates.
